chunks.heading: We always want more
chunks.body: People's wants never run out. As soon as one want is satisfied, a new one takes its place.
chunks.checkText: What happens once we satisfy one want?

chunks.heading: Resources are limited
chunks.body: The resources we use to make goods and services, like land, workers and machines, are limited. There's never enough for everyone to have everything.
chunks.checkText: What does it mean for a resource to be "scarce"?

checkOptions.text: There's only a limited amount of it
There's an unlimited amount of it

chunks.heading: The economic problem
chunks.body: The economic problem is that our [[econ-wants-unlimited|wants are unlimited]] but our [[econ-resources-scarce|resources are limited]]. This forces us to choose.
chunks.checkText: The economic problem is the clash between...

checkOptions.text: Too much money and too few shops

chunks.heading: Choosing means missing out
chunks.body: Because we can't satisfy every want, we must rank them and pick our top choices. Some wants get left unsatisfied.
chunks.checkText: Why must we rank our wants in order of priority?

checkOptions.text: Because we cannot satisfy them all
Because all wants cost the same

chunks.heading: Needs and wants
chunks.body: Needs are the basics we must have to survive, like food and shelter. Wants are everything else we'd like to have, but don't strictly need.
chunks.checkText: Which of these is a need, not a want?

chunks.heading: Wants that are personal
chunks.body: Individual wants are the things one person desires. They depend on that person's own income, age and taste.
chunks.checkText: Individual wants mainly depend on...

checkOptions.text: The person's own circumstances, like income

chunks.heading: Wants shared by everyone
chunks.body: Collective wants are things the whole community needs, like parks, schools and hospitals. Governments usually provide these.
chunks.checkText: Collective wants are usually provided by...

chunks.heading: The real cost of a choice
chunks.body: Opportunity cost is the next-best thing you give up when you choose something else. It's the true cost of a choice, not just its price.
chunks.checkText: Opportunity cost is best described as...

checkOptions.text: The next-best alternative you give up
The price tag on an item

chunks.heading: Four questions every economy must answer
chunks.body: Every economy must decide what to produce, how much to produce, how to produce it, and how to share it out among people.
chunks.checkText: Which is NOT one of the four key economic questions?

chunks.heading: Goods for now, goods for later
chunks.body: Consumer goods satisfy wants right away, like food. Capital goods, like machinery, aren't used directly but help produce more goods in the future.
chunks.checkText: A factory machine is an example of a...

chunks.heading: Today's choices shape tomorrow
chunks.body: Choosing to save money, study, or build [[econ-consumer-capital-goods|capital goods]] instead of spending now can mean a better outcome later, trading a bit of now for more later.
chunks.checkText: Choosing to study instead of working right away is an example of...

checkOptions.text: Sacrificing now to gain more later
A choice with no future effect

chunks.heading: What shapes an economic choice
chunks.body: Individuals, businesses and governments all weigh things like cost, income and future plans before making an economic choice.
chunks.checkText: Individuals, businesses and governments all consider what before choosing?

chunks.heading: A picture of possible choices
chunks.body: A production possibility frontier is a graph showing every combination of two goods an economy could produce with its current resources.
chunks.checkText: A production possibility frontier shows combinations of...

checkOptions.text: Two goods that can be produced
Every good in the economy at once

chunks.heading: The line means "fully used"
chunks.body: Every point sitting on the [[econ-ppf-intro|frontier]] line shows the economy using all its resources at once, with nothing wasted.
chunks.checkText: Points sitting exactly on the frontier line represent...

checkOptions.text: Points that are impossible to reach

chunks.heading: Moving along the frontier
chunks.body: To produce more of one good on the [[econ-ppf-intro|frontier]], you must produce less of the other. That drop is the [[econ-opportunity-cost|opportunity cost]] of the choice.
chunks.checkText: Moving along a production possibility frontier to get more of one good means...

checkOptions.text: Producing less of the other good

chunks.heading: Inside the line means wasted resources
chunks.body: A point sitting inside the [[econ-ppf-intro|frontier]] means some resources aren't being used, like unemployed workers. The economy could produce more.
chunks.checkText: A point inside the production possibility frontier shows that...

checkOptions.text: The economy is at maximum output

chunks.heading: Better technology moves the line out
chunks.body: New technology lets an economy produce more with the same resources. This pushes the whole [[econ-ppf-intro|frontier]] outward.
chunks.checkText: Better technology causes the production possibility frontier to...

chunks.heading: More resources moves the line out
chunks.body: Discovering new resources, or gaining more workers, also pushes the [[econ-ppf-intro|frontier]] outward, because there's more available to produce with.
chunks.checkText: An increase in the number of available workers would cause the frontier to...

chunks.heading: Why the line curves
chunks.body: A straight [[econ-ppf-intro|frontier]] assumes resources swap between goods at a constant rate. In reality, resources suit one good better than another, so the line curves inward instead.
chunks.checkText: A curved production possibility frontier reflects the fact that...

checkOptions.text: Resources aren't equally suited to producing both goods

chunks.heading: Letting the market decide
chunks.body: In a market economy, individuals and businesses make all the economic decisions themselves, motivated by their own self-interest.
chunks.checkText: In a market economy, who makes the main economic decisions?

chunks.heading: Letting the government decide
chunks.body: In a centrally planned economy, government planners decide what gets produced and how it's shared out, instead of individuals choosing.
chunks.checkText: In a centrally planned economy, decisions are mostly made by...

chunks.heading: A bit of both
chunks.body: A mixed economy combines [[econ-market-economy|market forces]] with some government decision-making. Australia is a mixed economy.
chunks.checkText: A mixed economy combines...

chunks.heading: Prices send a message
chunks.body: The price mechanism is how rising and falling prices match what buyers want with what sellers supply, guiding what gets produced.
chunks.checkText: The price mechanism works by using...

checkOptions.text: Changes in price to guide supply and demand

chunks.heading: What a market actually is
chunks.body: A market is simply buyers and sellers coming together to trade a particular good, service or resource at some price.
chunks.checkText: A market is best described as...

chunks.heading: The right to own things
chunks.body: In a [[econ-market-economy|market economy]], people can own resources and property, and can use them, sell them, or pass them on however they choose.
chunks.checkText: Private ownership of property means people can...

checkOptions.text: Own, use and sell their resources

chunks.heading: Consumers are in charge
chunks.body: Consumer sovereignty means consumers decide what gets produced, because businesses only make what people are willing to buy.
chunks.checkText: Consumer sovereignty means that, ultimately, production is decided by...

chunks.heading: Free to start a business
chunks.body: Freedom of enterprise means people can set up their own business and choose what to produce, without the government stopping them.
chunks.checkText: Freedom of enterprise allows individuals to...

checkOptions.text: Start and run their own business

chunks.heading: Why lots of sellers helps buyers
chunks.body: Competition happens when there are many buyers and sellers, so no single one can control the price. This helps keep prices fair.
chunks.checkText: Competition in a market helps keep prices...

checkOptions.text: Fair, because no single seller controls them

chunks.heading: Reason 1: some goods need government help
chunks.body: Governments sometimes provide goods like roads or defence because private businesses wouldn't supply them well on their own.
chunks.checkText: One reason governments get involved in the economy is to...

checkOptions.text: Provide goods the market wouldn't supply well
Stop all private businesses from operating

chunks.heading: Goods people undervalue
chunks.body: Merit goods are things like education or the arts that people don't buy enough of on their own, so governments help support them.
chunks.checkText: Merit goods are goods that...

checkOptions.text: The private market tends to under-provide

chunks.heading: Reason 2: sharing output more fairly
chunks.body: Governments also step in to redistribute income, for example through welfare payments and taxes, since the free market alone can leave some people with very little.
chunks.checkText: Redistributing income through welfare and taxes is an example of the government trying to...

checkOptions.text: Make the distribution of income fairer

chunks.heading: Reason 3: smoothing the ups and downs
chunks.body: Governments also intervene to reduce the swings of the [[econ-business-cycle|business cycle]], trying to keep the economy more stable over time.
chunks.checkText: A third reason governments intervene in the economy is to...

checkOptions.text: Smooth out swings in economic activity

chunks.heading: Comparing how well economies are doing
chunks.body: Economists compare countries using GDP per person, which measures the average value of goods and services produced per person in a year.
chunks.checkText: GDP per person is used to compare...

checkOptions.text: Only how many people live there

chunks.heading: Measuring more than money
chunks.body: The Human Development Index combines income, life expectancy and education levels to give a broader picture of quality of life than income alone.
chunks.checkText: The Human Development Index measures quality of life using...

checkOptions.text: Income, life expectancy and education together

chunks.heading: Goods you can touch, services you can't
chunks.body: Goods are physical things like food or cars. Services are actions that help you, like a doctor's visit or a haircut.
chunks.checkText: Which of these is a service, not a good?

chunks.heading: The four ingredients of production
chunks.body: Every good or service needs four resources to make it: natural resources, labour, capital and enterprise. These are called factors of production.
chunks.checkText: How many factors of production are there?

chunks.heading: Resources from nature
chunks.body: Natural resources are things like land, water and minerals that occur naturally and get used in production. Their reward is called rent.
chunks.checkText: The reward for supplying natural resources is called...

chunks.heading: Human effort at work
chunks.body: Labour is the physical and mental effort people put into producing goods and services. Workers are rewarded with wages.
chunks.checkText: The reward for supplying labour is called...

chunks.heading: Tools that help make more
chunks.body: Capital means things like machines and tools that are used to produce other goods, rather than being consumed directly. Its reward is interest.
chunks.checkText: A factory machine is an example of which factor of production?

chunks.heading: The person who takes the risk
chunks.body: Enterprise is the skill of organising the other resources and taking the risk of running a business. Its reward is profit.
chunks.checkText: The reward for enterprise is called...

chunks.heading: How market economies share output
chunks.body: In a market economy, people get a share of goods based on the income they earn, which depends on the resources they supply.
chunks.checkText: In a market economy, how much of total output a person gets mostly depends on...

chunks.heading: Why we use money to trade
chunks.body: Money makes trading goods and services much easier, because it means you don't need to find someone who wants exactly what you're offering.
chunks.checkText: Using money instead of trading goods directly mainly helps because...

checkOptions.text: You don't need to match wants exactly

chunks.heading: Trading goods without money
chunks.body: Barter is swapping one good or service directly for another, without using money at all. It's rare in modern economies.
chunks.checkText: Barter means...

chunks.heading: The economy moves in cycles
chunks.body: The business cycle describes how economic activity rises and falls over time, instead of growing at a steady, constant rate.
chunks.checkText: The business cycle refers to...

checkOptions.text: Ups and downs in economic activity over time

chunks.heading: When the economy shrinks
chunks.body: A recession is a period when economic activity falls, production drops, and unemployment tends to rise.
chunks.checkText: During a recession, unemployment tends to...

chunks.heading: When the economy is booming
chunks.body: A boom is a period of strong economic growth, when production rises and unemployment tends to fall.
chunks.checkText: During an economic boom, production tends to...

chunks.heading: A model of the whole economy
chunks.body: The circular flow of income is a model that splits the economy into sectors, showing how money moves between them.
chunks.checkText: The circular flow of income model is used to show...

checkOptions.text: How money moves between sectors of the economy
The weather patterns of a country

chunks.heading: Individuals and businesses need each other
chunks.body: Individuals supply resources like [[econ-labour|labour]] to businesses and earn income in return. Businesses use that income by selling goods back to individuals.
chunks.checkText: In the circular flow, individuals supply businesses with...

chunks.heading: Where savings go to work
chunks.body: Financial institutions, like banks, collect savings from individuals and lend that money to businesses so they can invest.
chunks.checkText: Financial institutions mainly act as a link between...

chunks.heading: Government's role in the flow
chunks.body: Governments collect taxes from individuals and businesses, then spend that money on things like schools, hospitals and roads.
chunks.checkText: Governments fund their spending mainly through...

chunks.heading: Money moving across borders
chunks.body: The international sector covers trade with other countries: exports, which are goods sold overseas, and imports, which are goods bought from overseas.
chunks.checkText: Exports are goods and services that are...

chunks.heading: Money leaving the flow
chunks.body: Leakages are money that leaves the circular flow, through savings, taxes, or imports, reducing the level of economic activity.
chunks.checkText: Which of these is an example of a leakage?

chunks.heading: Money entering the flow
chunks.body: Injections are money entering the circular flow, through investment, government spending, or exports, increasing the level of economic activity.
chunks.checkText: Which of these is an example of an injection?

chunks.heading: When the flow is balanced
chunks.body: The circular flow is in equilibrium when total [[econ-leakages|leakages]] equal total [[econ-injections|injections]], keeping the level of economic activity steady.
chunks.checkText: The circular flow is in equilibrium when...

checkOptions.text: Injections are always bigger than leakages
